title: Packet Storm
description: Packet Storm is the 1982 fifth album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of classic heavy metal about how computers talk to each other. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Byt plays lead guitar, and Bytes plays drums and sings backup. Packet switching, the seven layers, Ethernet collisions, addresses and ports, routing, the three-way handshake, sequence numbers, packet loss, UDP, congestion control, name servers, and the day the whole network switched to TCP/IP at once. Recorded in three different cities and sent by mail, one reel at a time. Some arrived out of order. One never arrived. Play loud. Acknowledge receipt.
tagline: The 1982 heavy metal album from Procedural Byts: a networking course in twelve songs, recorded by mail and reassembled by sequence number.
lineup: Still a power trio, now in three different cities. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass guitar. Byt plays lead guitar. Bytes plays drums and sings backup.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits and the band’s protocol. Nyble sings lead on every song, plays bass, and insisted on a three-letter handshake before anyone mailed anything.

members.name: Byt
members.bio: One bit, back on guitar for every song, and speaking to the others again by the end of the sessions. Byt’s solos on this record chop melodies into packets, hop them between instruments, and resend anything that goes missing.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, and the reason the engineer learned to number tape reels. Bytes plays drums and sings backup, and his solo on Sequence Number puts his own scrambled fills back in order.

members.name: Null
members.bio: Shipped with the master tapes on every delivery. Arrived in order every time, which is more than anyone else managed.

story.heading: Recorded by Mail
paragraphs: After Syntax Error, the band spent 1981 in three different cities. Byt was still not discussing Side B. So when it came time to make an album about networks, they decided to record it over one: the postal service.

Each member recorded their parts at home and mailed the reels to the studio. Before any tape could be sent, Nyble insisted on a handshake: a letter asking “ready to receive?”, a reply saying “ready, are you?”, and a third letter saying “sending.” It took six weeks before a single note crossed the country.

Bytes’s drum reels arrived out of order, so the engineer numbered every reel and reassembled them by sequence number. Two reels arrived twice and were thrown out. One never arrived at all, and after three weeks with no word, Bytes recorded it again. That became Packet Loss.
Byt’s tapes went through four post offices on the way to the studio, one of them in the wrong country. He wrote Router of the Lost while he waited.
Null traveled in the box with the master tapes as packing material, there and back, on every single shipment. It is the most-traveled duck in rock.

The closer, Flag Day, was written for January 1, 1983, when the whole network switched to TCP/IP at the same moment. The band was finally back in one room to record it, which Nyble says was the real flag day.

cover_sub: The fifth album, 1982. Recorded in three cities and sent by mail, one reel at a time.

songs.title: Packet Storm

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A message much too large to send, a mountain made of words,
Break it into pieces and scatter them like birds.
Every piece a packet with a header on its head,
Where it’s from and where it’s going, and the number that it said!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Packet storm! (Packet storm!)
Thousands in the night!
Packet storm! (Packet storm!)
Every piece takes its own flight!
Different roads and different times, they gather at the door,
Packet storm, and the message lives once more!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The telephone would hold a line from the start until the end,
A circuit just for you and me, and no one else to send.
But packets share the wire, a crowd upon the road,
Nobody owns the highway, everybody shares the load!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Circuit switched! (A line for one!)
Packet switched! (A line for everyone!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt chops a long melody into short numbered fragments and sends some through Nyble’s bass and some through Bytes’s toms, out of order. In the last bars every fragment has arrived, and he plays the whole melody through, reassembled.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Packet storm! (Packet storm!)
Thousands in the night!
Packet storm! (Packet storm!)
Every piece takes its own flight!
Different roads and different times, they gather at the door,
Packet storm, and the message lives once more!

songs.note: The storm at the start is three tape decks playing static at once.
songs.lesson: Packet switching splits data into packets, each with a header saying where it came from, where it’s going and where it fits. Packets travel independently, possibly by different routes, and are reassembled at the far end. Unlike circuit switching, which reserves a whole line for one conversation like an old telephone call, packets share the links, which makes networks efficient and hard to knock out.

songs.title: Seven Layers Deep

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Down at the bottom, the wire and the light,
Ones and zeros sent as voltage through the night.
Above it is the link that talks from node to node,
Then the network finds the path along the road!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Seven layers deep! (Wrap it up!)
Seven layers deep! (Unwrap it up!)
Every layer has a job and wraps the one below,
Seven layers deep, and that’s the way it goes!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Transport keeps it reliable, it numbers every part,
Session, presentation, then the app, the beating heart.
On the way down, wrap it, a header at each stage,
On the way up, unwrap it, turn back every page!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Physical! Data link! Network! Transport!
(Session!) (Presentation!) Application!

parts.label: Instrumental break: full band
parts.desc: Byt plays a simple melody. Nyble wraps a bass line around it, and Bytes wraps a drum part around both, layer by layer. Then they unwrap it in reverse until only Byt’s melody is left, delivered.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Seven layers deep! (Wrap it up!)
Seven layers deep! (Unwrap it up!)
Every layer has a job and wraps the one below,
Seven layers deep, and that’s the way it goes!

songs.note: The longest song on the album, wrapped seven times.
songs.lesson: Networks are built in layers: the OSI model has seven (physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application), and the internet uses the simpler TCP/IP stack. Each layer serves the one above it and uses the one below. Sending wraps the data in each layer’s header on the way down (encapsulation), and receiving unwraps them in reverse.

songs.title: Collision Domain

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: One cable for the whole floor, one hall where all can talk,
Listen first, and if it’s quiet, then you take the walk.
But two can hear the silence and both begin to send,
They crash upon the wire, and the message meets its end!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Collision domain! (Crash!)
Two at once and the signals clash!
Back off, back off, wait a random time,
Then try again, and maybe this time you’ll be fine!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Every card has an address burned in at the start,
A hardware name six bytes long to tell the cards apart.
Frames go out with that address so the right one hears the call,
The others hear it passing and ignore it, one and all!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Carrier sense! (Listen first!)
Collision detect! (Expect the worst!)

parts.label: Trading solo: Byt and Nyble
parts.desc: Byt and Nyble start solos at the same instant and crash into each other. Both stop, wait a random number of beats, and try again. It takes three tries before one of them gets the wire to themselves.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Collision domain! (Crash!)
Two at once and the signals clash!
Back off, back off, wait a random time,
Then try again, and maybe this time you’ll be fine!

songs.note: Byt and Nyble started the solo at the same time on every take. Eventually they made that the song.
songs.lesson: In classic Ethernet, every device shares one wire. With CSMA/CD, a device listens before sending, detects when two transmissions collide, and retries after a random backoff. Every network card has a unique 48-bit MAC address, which is used to deliver frames on the local network.

songs.title: Address Unknown

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Four numbers and three dots, that’s the address of a host,
Every machine on the network has the one it needs the most.
The first part names the network and the rest names the machine,
A street and then a house number, the finest map you’ve seen!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Address unknown! (Where do you live?)
Address unknown! (What can you give?)
Four numbers find the machine, a port to find the door,
Address unknown, till I know what I’m looking for!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The address finds the computer, but which program will it be?
The port picks out the one inside that’s waiting there for me.
Address and port together make a socket on the line,
Two sockets make a conversation, yours connected to mine!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: One twenty-seven! (That’s home!)
No address at all! (Unknown!)

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble’s solo is four short phrases, each narrowing the range: the first picks the octave, the next the string, then the fret, then the exact note. That’s the address. The last note she holds is the port.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Address unknown! (Where do you live?)
Address unknown! (What can you give?)
Four numbers find the machine, a port to find the door,
Address unknown, till I know what I’m looking for!

songs.note: The four-note chant in the chorus is a real address. The band won’t say whose.
songs.lesson: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number written as four numbers separated by dots. Part of it identifies the network and the rest identifies the host. A port number picks which program on that host gets the data, and an address plus a port makes a socket; a connection joins two sockets. 127.0.0.1 always means “this machine.”

songs.title: Router of the Lost

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A packet stands at the crossroads and it doesn’t know the way,
The router reads the address and sends it on its way.
It doesn’t know the whole road, just the next hop down the line,
Hop by hop across the world, it gets there just in time!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Router of the lost! (Next hop!)
Router of the lost! (Never stop!)
Read the table, pick the path, and send it out the door,
Router of the lost, and it’s closer than before!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The routers talk among themselves, they share what they have learned,
Which links are fast, which links are down, which bridges have been burned.
They find the shortest path, and when a cable has been cut,
They route around the damage, and they never hit a rut!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Time to live! (Count it down!)
Too many hops and the packet’s drowned!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt hands the melody to Nyble, who hands it to Bytes, who hands it back, each one moving it closer to the final key. Once, it takes a wrong turn and bounces around too many times, and the band lets it die out: time to live.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Router of the lost! (Next hop!)
Router of the lost! (Never stop!)
Read the table, pick the path, and send it out the door,
Router of the lost, and it’s closer than before!

songs.note: Byt’s master tapes went through four post offices to reach the studio, one of them in the wrong country.
songs.lesson: Routers forward packets hop by hop, using routing tables that map destinations to the next hop. Routing protocols let routers share what they know about links so they can find good (often shortest) paths and route around failures. Each packet carries a time-to-live counter that drops at every hop, so a lost packet can’t circle forever.

songs.title: Three-Way Handshake

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Before we talk, we greet, and before we send, we meet,
A knock upon the door, three steps to make it complete.
I send you SYN, a sync, a number of my own,
Then you send it back with yours, and now the seeds are sown!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Three-way handshake! (SYN!)
Three-way handshake! (SYN-ACK!)
Three-way handshake! (ACK!)
And now we’re connected, and there’s no turning back!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Each side picks a number for the bytes that it will send,
And both sides must agree before the message can begin.
Then when the talk is over, we say goodbye with care,
A FIN from me, a FIN from you, and nothing left in there!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Connection-oriented! (Hand in hand!)
Reliable from end to end! (That’s the plan!)

parts.label: Call-and-answer solo: Byt and Nyble
parts.desc: Byt plays a phrase: SYN. Nyble answers it and adds her own: SYN-ACK. Byt confirms with a single chord: ACK. Only then do they launch into the solo together, connected.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Three-way handshake! (SYN!)
Three-way handshake! (SYN-ACK!)
Three-way handshake! (ACK!)
And now we’re connected, and there’s no turning back!

songs.note: Every package the band mailed during the sessions needed three letters first. This song is those letters.
songs.lesson: TCP sets up a connection with a three-way handshake: the client sends SYN with its starting sequence number, the server replies SYN-ACK with its own, and the client confirms with ACK. Both sides agree on numbering before any data flows. When they’re done, each side sends FIN to close the connection.

songs.title: Sequence Number

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The packets come in scrambled, three, then one, then two,
Every one took its own road, and that’s what roads will do.
But every one is numbered, so I put them back in line,
One, two, three, and the message reads exactly fine!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Sequence number! (Count them in!)
Sequence number! (Where they’ve been!)
Number every byte you send and acknowledge what you get,
Sequence number, and the order isn’t lost yet!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: I send you bytes, you tell me what you’ve got so far,
An ACK for each arrival says exactly where we are.
A duplicate arrives, I throw the extra out,
The numbers tell me everything, and there’s never any doubt!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Out of order! (Sort it out!)
Duplicate! (Throw it out!)

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays six drum fills in scrambled order. Nyble counts them off by number, one through six, and he plays them again in sequence. The second time, they make a single long fill that was there all along.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Sequence number! (Count them in!)
Sequence number! (Where they’ve been!)
Number every byte you send and acknowledge what you get,
Sequence number, and the order isn’t lost yet!

songs.note: Bytes’s drum tapes really did arrive out of order. This song is how they put them back.
songs.lesson: TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses these sequence numbers to put data back in order and throw away duplicates, and sends acknowledgments (ACKs) saying what has arrived. Together they turn a network that can scramble and duplicate packets into an ordered, reliable stream.

songs.title: Packet Loss

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I sent it out at midnight and I’m waiting by the line,
No answer from the other side, no acknowledgment, no sign.
Maybe it was lost in a storm, maybe dropped along the way,
The timer’s running down, and I can’t wait another day!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Packet loss! (Gone!)
Somewhere in the night!
Packet loss! (Gone!)
Send it again and get it right!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The network makes no promises, it does the best it can,
A full queue drops the extras and a noisy wire will jam.
The sender keeps a copy till it knows the copy’s home,
Retransmit what’s missing, and you’re never on your own!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Timeout! (Timeout!) Send it again!
Retransmit! (Retransmit!) Until the end!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Every so often one of Byt’s phrases drops out into silence. He waits for Nyble’s nod that it arrived, and when the nod doesn’t come, he plays the missing phrase again until it does.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Packet loss! (Gone!)
Somewhere in the night!
Packet loss! (Gone!)
Send it again and get it right!

Packet loss, packet loss, till it reaches you, my friend!

songs.note: One of Bytes’s reels never arrived. He waited three weeks, then recorded it again.
songs.lesson: Networks are best-effort: packets get dropped when router queues fill up, or get corrupted on noisy links. TCP keeps a copy of everything not yet acknowledged and runs a retransmission timer. If no ACK arrives in time, it sends the data again. That retransmission is how TCP stays reliable over an unreliable network.

songs.title: Fire and Forget

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: No handshake, no waiting, no numbers on the side,
Just throw it at the address and let it take the ride.
If it gets there, great, and if it doesn’t, never mind,
Fire and forget, I never look behind!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Fire and forget! (UDP!)
Fire and forget! (Fast and free!)
No promise that it gets there, no promise of the order,
Fire and forget, straight across the border!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: For a voice that cannot wait, for a game that’s moving fast,
A late packet is worthless, so let the old ones pass.
Small and quick and simple, a header thin and light,
When speed beats perfection, it’s the protocol that’s right!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: TCP! (Reliable but slow!)
UDP! (Just let it go!)

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays the fastest fills of his life and never goes back to fix a missed hit. A few notes vanish in the blur. Nobody notices, because by then he’s three bars ahead.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Fire and forget! (UDP!)
Fire and forget! (Fast and free!)
No promise that it gets there, no promise of the order,
Fire and forget, straight across the border!

songs.note: The fastest song the band recorded in the 1980s. No second takes, on principle.
songs.lesson: UDP sends datagrams with no connection setup, no acknowledgments, no ordering and no retransmission. That means very little overhead and low delay, but no guarantee of delivery. It suits real-time voice, video and games, where late data is useless, and quick lookups. TCP trades speed for reliability and order.

songs.title: Slow Start

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Start with a single packet and see if it gets through,
Then two, then four, then eight, the window doubles too.
The road is wide, the road is fast, and no one’s in the way,
Faster, faster, faster, till the network starts to sway!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Slow start! (Double it up!)
Slow start! (Fill the cup!)
But when a packet’s lost it means the road is jammed,
Back off, cut it in half, or the whole network’s damned!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The receiver has a window that says how much it can take,
Don’t flood it with more data than its buffers were built to make.
And the network has its limits, every router has its queue,
Push too hard and everybody’s slow, including you!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Flow control! (Don’t drown the one you send to!)
Congestion control! (Don’t drown the road you’re on too!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt starts with one note per bar, then two, then four, then eight, until the amp starts to distort. He cuts back to half and climbs again, one note at a time this time, staying just under the edge.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Slow start! (Double it up!)
Slow start! (Fill the cup!)
But when a packet’s lost it means the road is jammed,
Back off, cut it in half, or the whole network’s damned!

songs.note: The only song where the band deliberately starts quiet. It doesn’t last.
songs.lesson: Flow control, through the receiver’s window, keeps a sender from overwhelming the receiver. Congestion control keeps senders from overwhelming the network. TCP’s slow start doubles the sending window every round trip; when packets are lost, it cuts the window in half and then grows it slowly again.

songs.title: Name Server

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Nobody remembers numbers, four of them in a row,
We remember names, and the names are all we know.
Once there was a single file with every host inside,
But the network kept on growing and the file got too wide!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Name server! (Who are you?)
Name server! (Tell me true!)
Give it a name and it gives you back a number,
Name server, wake the network from its slumber!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Split the names in pieces, a hierarchy of trees,
Ask the root and it points you on, down the branches, if you please.
Every zone has its own server, every server knows its part,
Cache the answer for a while and you’ll get a running start!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Dot! (The root!) The domain! (The branch!)
The host! (The leaf!) And the number in your hand!

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble plays a phrase that sounds like a name, and Bytes answers with a rhythmic pattern: its number. The second time she plays the name, he doesn’t answer, because she already remembers it: cached.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Name server! (Who are you?)
Name server! (Tell me true!)
Give it a name and it gives you back a number,
Name server, wake the network from its slumber!

songs.note: In 1982 every computer on the network kept a list of every other computer’s name, in one file. This song is about why that couldn’t last.
songs.lesson: People use names, and networks use numeric addresses. Early on, every machine kept one shared hosts file listing every other machine, which couldn’t keep up as the network grew. The Domain Name System, introduced in 1983 and 1984, is a distributed, hierarchical directory: a lookup starts at the root, is pointed down through the domains to an authoritative answer, and the result is cached for a while.

songs.title: Flag Day

parts.label: Intro (spoken)
lines: On January first, every machine on the network had to change its language at the same time.
Nobody was allowed to be late.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Midnight on the first of the year and every machine must change,
The old protocol is dying and the new one feels strange.
TCP and IP together on the line,
Every network joining every other, all at the same time!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Flag day! (Raise it high!)
Flag day! (Networks multiply!)
A network made of networks, all speaking one tongue,
Flag day, flag day, and the internet is young!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Clients ask the questions and the servers give replies,
Protocols are promises that everyone abides.
Agree on what the bytes mean and the world can talk as one,
Different wires and different machines, a single language spun!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Internetwork! (A network of networks!)
Every wire! (And every word!)

parts.label: Cutover: full band
parts.desc: The band plays the old riff together, faster and faster. On a single crash from Bytes, all three switch to a completely new riff at the exact same instant, and nobody is late.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Flag day! (Raise it high!)
Flag day! (Networks multiply!)
A network made of networks, all speaking one tongue,
Flag day, flag day, and the internet is young!

songs.note: Written for January 1, 1983, the day the whole network switched to TCP/IP at once.
songs.lesson: The internet is a network of networks joined by shared protocols. On January 1, 1983, the ARPANET switched to TCP/IP all at once, a cutover known as flag day. Protocols are agreements about message formats and behavior, and client-server is the most common pattern: clients send requests and servers respond.
